title: Most Expensive Item That Can Not Be Bought
statement:
A shop has an item at every positive integer price. You hold an unlimited supply of coins worth `primeOne` and coins worth `primeTwo`, which are two different prime numbers. An item can be bought only when its price equals some total of these coins exactly, using each coin value any number of times (possibly zero). No change is given.

Return the highest price of an item that cannot be bought. Because the two primes share no common factor, only finitely many prices are out of reach, so this price always exists.
constraints: primeOne and primeTwo are prime numbers
notes:
## Intuition

A direct method marks which prices from 0 up to `primeOne * primeTwo` can be paid (a price is payable when the price minus one coin is) and reports the highest unmarked one. Number theory gives the answer without any table.

Sort prices into `primeOne` classes by their remainder modulo `primeOne`. Adding a `primeOne` coin keeps a price in its class, so once a class has one payable price, every higher price in that class is payable. Using `j` coins of `primeTwo` for `j = 0, 1, ..., primeOne - 1` lands in a different class each time (the primes are distinct, hence coprime), and `j * primeTwo` is the cheapest payable price of its class. The class reached last starts at `(primeOne - 1) * primeTwo`; the price one `primeOne` step below it is out of reach, and everything above it is payable. That price is `primeOne * primeTwo - primeOne - primeTwo`.

## Approach

1. There are `classes = primeOne` remainder classes.
2. The last class to be reached needs `lastCount = classes - 1` coins of `primeTwo`.
3. Its cheapest payable price is `lastReached = lastCount * primeTwo`.
4. Step one coin of `primeOne` below it: `largest = lastReached - primeOne` is the answer.

## Example 1, step by step

`primeOne = 2`, `primeTwo = 5`: `classes = 2` (even and odd prices), `lastCount = 1`, `lastReached = 5` (the first odd payable price) and `largest = 5 - 2 = 3`. Indeed 1 and 3 cannot be paid, while 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and everything higher can.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1): a few multiplications.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- The answer is symmetric in the two primes; no need to order them.
- The formula needs the coin values to be coprime; equal primes would leave infinitely many prices unpayable, which is why the primes are distinct.
- A price of 0 (buying nothing) is not an item; the answer is always at least 1.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `classes` | number of remainder classes modulo `primeOne` |
| `lastCount` | coins of `primeTwo` needed to reach the last class |
| `lastReached` | cheapest payable price in that last class |
| `largest` | the most expensive price that cannot be paid |

narration.1: The two coin values are distinct primes, so they share no common factor.
narration.2: Group prices by their remainder modulo primeOne; adding a primeOne coin never changes the group.
narration.3: Taking 0, 1, ..., primeOne - 1 coins of primeTwo reaches every group once, so the last group needs primeOne - 1 of them.
narration.4: This is the cheapest payable price in the last group; every higher price in it is payable too.
narration.5: One primeOne coin below it is the highest price that no combination can pay.
narration.6: Return that price, which equals primeOne * primeTwo - primeOne - primeTwo.
